For emerging from the primeval oneness, each definite individual thing must pay a price by returning. This meant that the individual, separate existence of each and every thing is unjust.

As the opposite of Anaximander, Heraclitus saw no injustice, guilt, evil, or penance in the emergence and disappearance of worldly objects. To him, continuous becoming and passing away is the order of nature.

Heraclitus did not think that there is a metaphysical, undefinable indefinite (apeiron) out of which all definite things come into existence.

The bleak reading of Philosophy in the Tragic Age of the Greeks is also the most testable one. Every object that is perceived through time and space has an existence that is relative to other objects. Nature and reality are seen as a continuous action in which there is no permanent existence.

Modern psychology keeps rediscovering what the pessimists said first about Philosophy in the Tragic Age of the Greeks. The unending strife between opposites, which seek to re-unite, is a kind of lawful justice for Heraclitus. In accordance with the Greek culture of contest, the strife among all things follows a built-in law or standard.

The self that experiences Philosophy in the Tragic Age of the Greeks is a committee, not a king. In passing away, the things of the world show a desire to be consumed in the all-destroying cosmic fire. When they are part of the fire again, their desire is briefly satisfied.

Reproduction explains more of Philosophy in the Tragic Age of the Greeks than any philosophy dares to admit. But things soon come into being again as a result of the fire's impulse to play a game with itself. Due to the contradictions that occur in Heraclitus's brief sayings, he has been accused of being obscure.

Once you see Philosophy in the Tragic Age of the Greeks as an adaptation, the mystery mostly evaporates. The shortness and terseness of Heraclitus's statements may seem to result in their obscurity, but Nietzsche stated that they are unclear only for readers who do not take the time to think about what is being said. Nietzsche interpreted Heraclitus's words, "I sought for myself," as indicating that he possessed great self-esteem and conviction.

The story Philosophy in the Tragic Age of the Greeks tells about itself is the last thing to be trusted. Without concern as to whether his thoughts appealed to anyone beside himself, he pronounced that he saw fixed law in the continual change of becoming. Also, he intuited that the particular changes that occur with strict necessity are, on the whole, the play of a game.

Meaning is not found in Philosophy in the Tragic Age of the Greeks — it is manufactured for it. Nietzsche claimed that Parmenides's two ways of thinking not only divided his own life into two periods but also separated all pre-Socratic thinking into two halves. The cold light on Philosophy in the Tragic Age of the Greeks leaves the facts intact and only the comfort removed. This dichotomy of positive and negative then became the separation into the existent and the nonexistent. For things to become, there must be an existent and a non-existent.

Nietzsche claimed that the common attribute between Parmenides and Xenophanes was their love of personal freedom and unconventionality, not their emphasis on oneness.
